title: The Theorem of Pythagoras
summary: Use the Theorem of Pythagoras to calculate a missing side of a right-angled triangle, use its converse to test whether a triangle is right-angled, and solve practical problems.

notes.text: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite the right angle is called the **hypotenuse**. It is always the **longest** side. The other two sides are sometimes called the legs.

notes.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15"><g fill="none" stroke="#000" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="60,40 60,160 220,160"/><polyline points="60,146 74,146 74,160" stroke-width="1.5"/></g><g fill="#000"><text x="52" y="32">A</text><text x="44" y="176">B</text><text x="224" y="176">C</text><text x="40" y="105">3</text><text x="135" y="182">4</text><text x="150" y="92" font-size="13">5 (hypotenuse)</text></g></svg>
notes.caption: Triangle ABC with a right angle at B. The hypotenuse AC is opposite the right angle. Here AB = 3, BC = 4 and AC = 5.

notes.text: The Greek mathematician Pythagoras is credited with discovering that, in **every** right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

notes.caption: Theorem of Pythagoras for triangle ABC with the right angle at B (often written c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse)

notes.text: Check it with the triangle above: $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2$ ✓. If you draw a square on each side, the area of the biggest square ($25$) equals the total area of the other two squares ($9 + 16$).

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: The theorem only works for **right-angled** triangles. Always identify the hypotenuse first: it is opposite the right angle, and it is the side on its own on one side of the equation.

notes.title: Worked example 1
notes.problem: In $\triangle PQR$, $\hat{Q} = 90^\circ$, $PQ = 6$ cm and $QR = 8$ cm. Calculate $PR$.

notes.title: Worked example 2: an answer that is not a whole number
notes.problem: The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are 5 cm and 7 cm. Calculate the hypotenuse, correct to two decimal places.

notes.text: If you know the hypotenuse and one other side, **subtract**: $(\text{shorter side})^2 = (\text{hypotenuse})^2 - (\text{other side})^2$.

notes.title: Worked example 3
notes.problem: In $\triangle DEF$, $\hat{E} = 90^\circ$, $DF = 13$ cm and $DE = 5$ cm. Calculate $EF$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Adding when you should subtract. If your "shorter" side comes out **longer** than the hypotenuse, you added instead of subtracting. Also, $\sqrt{169 - 25} \neq 13 - 5$: work out the squares, subtract, then take the square root.

The theorem also works backwards: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the triangle **is** right-angled, and the right angle is opposite the longest side.

notes.title: Worked example 4
notes.problem: Are these triangles right-angled? (a) sides 7, 24, 25  (b) sides 4, 5, 6
steps: (b) Longest side $6$: $6^2 = 36$. Others: $4^2 + 5^2 = 16 + 25 = 41$. Not equal, so **no**.

notes.text: Three whole numbers that fit the theorem are called a **Pythagorean triple**: $(3;\ 4;\ 5)$, $(5;\ 12;\ 13)$, $(8;\ 15;\ 17)$, $(7;\ 24;\ 25)$. Multiples also work: $(6;\ 8;\ 10)$ and $(9;\ 12;\ 15)$ come from $(3;\ 4;\ 5)$.
Look for the right angle in real situations: a wall and the ground, the corner of a rectangle, the height of a triangle. Draw a sketch and label it.

notes.title: Worked example 5: a ladder
notes.problem: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 1,4 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The wall and ground meet at $90^\circ$, and the ladder is the hypotenuse.

notes.title: Worked example 6: a shortcut
notes.problem: A rectangular sports field is 40 m long and 30 m wide. How much shorter is it to walk diagonally across the field than along two edges?

items: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
Finding the hypotenuse: add the squares. Finding a shorter side: subtract the squares.
Square, then add or subtract, then take the square root (not the other way round).
Converse: if the longest side squared equals the sum of the other two squares, the triangle is right-angled.

options: The side next to the right angle
The side opposite the right angle
